extracted.intended_audience: students and readers interested in rhetoric, public speaking, and cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative guidance for public speaking/oratory across genres (stump speeches, lectures, commemorative orations, after-dinner speeches, parliamentary debate), describing what makes speeches effective or defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention (finding ideas and weaving arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention, that is to say, the power of finding good ideas and weaving effective arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance depends on the intellectual resources of the speaker and on the capacity of the audience for appreciating worthy matter. Good invention requires solid matter rather than ornament; not every occasion demands novelty of idea, but sound argumentation is essential when aiming to instruct or convince.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill and taste in choice of appropriate words
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill and taste in the choice of appropriate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clearness and cogency of expression to florid diction. Avoid overloading with tropes and ornament intended to conceal poverty of thought; language should suit the subject and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness (producing ideas and words at short notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness in producing appropriate ideas and words at short notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fluency and quickness of mind (self-possession) are valuable, especially in stump and after-dinner speaking. Readiness helps meet uncharted freedom (e.g., being called to 'offer a few remarks') and keeps the speaker responsive to the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quickness in reading the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Quickness in catching the temper and tendencies of the particular audience addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective speakers gauge audience sentiment and adapt tone, humour, and examples accordingly. This audience-sensitivity can increase effectiveness but may drag a speaker down if the audience is ignorant or prejudiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight, animation, and grace in delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight, animation, and grace in delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery should combine seriousness (weight) with animation and graceful manner. Manage physical action and vocal animation to rouse enthusiasm without vehemence or obvious posing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluency and self-possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluency, more readiness, more self-possession in delivery than mere literary finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fluency keeps the speaker's mind and audience in contact; self-possession prevents embarrassment on one's legs. These qualities often trump purely literary form in persuasive popular speaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance vs. literary form
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of speeches depends on the intellectual resources of the speaker and on the capacity of the audience; literary form (choicer language) is a separate concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake elegant language for substantive thought. Choose form to serve substance; if the audience values plainness, favour solid matter over ornamental phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humour to engage audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is the best means of keeping speaker and audience in touch and often redeems an otherwise uninteresting address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate anecdotes and lightness maintain attention, especially in American audiences; humour should be used to sustain rapport but not to evade argument where instruction or conviction is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery pace: deliberate and even slow delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate and even slow delivery often aids effectiveness; it makes a story or jest tell with more effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tempo should suit the occasion and material; slow, measured delivery can increase clarity and impact. Avoid frantic speed that sacrifices enunciation and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice management and clear enunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater skill in managing the voice and greater clearness of enunciation improve delivery, especially in open-air meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice projection and articulation; reduce stiffness and hesitation. Clear voice management helps reach large and diverse audiences and supports both humour and serious argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turgid, inflated, or florid rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid turgid and inflated style—rhetoric overloaded with tropes, ornament, and appeals loftier than the subject or occasion requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Florid diction often disguises thin thought. Prefer Attic/direct style (example given: Abraham Lincoln) — direct, clear, and sinewy phrasing produces stronger effects than ostentatious ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate finish and length for commemorative addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Commemorative addresses and orations of the occasion often err by over-finish and excessive length, becoming pompous and affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When speaking at anniversaries or unveilings, include good matter such as personal recollections but avoid artificial elevation and needless elaboration that wearies outsiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify purpose: stimulation vs instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize whether the speech's aim is to stimulate (stump oratory) or to instruct/convince (lectures, reasoned debate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stump oratory naturally seeks stimulation, using invective, stories, and jokes to rouse a partisan audience; lectures and instructive addresses should prioritize argument, arrangement, and meeting the audience's intellectual expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt presentation to venue and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different venues and genres (House, Senate, committees, mass meetings, conventions, lectures, after-dinner banquets) require different styles and aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., Senate benefits from leisure and smaller chamber for weighty oratory; House set speeches can be pompous; mass meetings reward flexible, entertaining delivery. Tailor length, tone, and formality to the setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oration of the Occasion: balance finish with relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Oration of the Occasion (anniversary, unveiling, monument openings) expects a long, highly finished harangue but risks being wearisome or pompous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide material of local or personal interest (recollections) and resist the temptation to sustain an artificial elevation of tone purely for form's sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: After-dinner / epideictic speaking: freedom and anecdote
rubrics_metrics.description: Complimentary, epideictic, and after-dinner speeches often have no prescribed subject and give the speaker a wide range for anecdote and wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the uncharted freedom to engage with anecdotes and humour; audiences will often listen courteously even to long-winded or late-night addresses, but adapt to the convivial context rather than formal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture standards: arrangement, composition, and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Lectures intended to instruct are usually well arranged, well composed to meet the taste of the audience, and, above all, well delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is instruction, structure the material clearly, respect audience expectations for sobriety (less applause/laughter), and deliver with attentive clarity to foster critical appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical 'claptrap'—seek reasoned argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on declamatory ornament or hearty conviction; effective oratory requires attempts to get hold of the reason and judgment of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when rousing sentiment, combine appeals with sound argument where possible; excessive invective and mere declamation impede the educational value of political campaigns and debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer transparent simplicity and directness
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent simplicity attains high effects by direct and natural methods rather than by ostentation (example: Wendell Phillips and Lincoln).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for directness and naturalness of expression to achieve the greatest rhetorical impact—simplicity often produces more effect than elaborate finish.
